title: Common Rashes in Babies and Kids
hook: Most childhood rashes — diaper rash, eczema, heat rash, hand-foot-and-mouth — are common and harmless. There's one big exception worth memorizing: a rash that doesn't fade when you press it.
key_points: Diaper rash is usually skin irritation from wetness; keep the area clean, dry, and air it out.
Eczema brings dry, itchy patches — moisturize often and avoid harsh soaps and triggers.
Heat rash (tiny bumps) and hand-foot-and-mouth (blisters, mouth sores) are common and usually mild.
Red flag: a rash that does NOT fade when pressed (the glass test) is an emergency — call 911/999.
content_html: Rashes are a normal part of babyhood, and the vast majority are harmless. Diaper rash is the classic one — usually irritant contact dermatitis, the skin reacting to contact with urine, stool, and a wet diaper rubbing against it. The American Academy of Pediatrics' main fixes are simple: change diapers promptly, keep the area clean and dry, give it some air, and use a barrier cream; a rash that lingers or looks different may be a yeast infection your doctor can treat.
extra_html: Other everyday rashes are similarly manageable: eczema shows up as dry, itchy patches and responds to frequent moisturizing and avoiding harsh soaps; heat rash is tiny bumps from being too warm; and hand-foot-and-mouth disease brings blisters and mouth sores but usually clears on its own. The one exception to memorize is the non-blanching rash: press a clear glass firmly against the spots, and if they do NOT fade — looking like small bruises or bleeding under the skin — treat it as an emergency and call 911 (or 999), because it can signal meningitis or sepsis. When a rash comes with high fever, a stiff neck, or a very unwell child, seek care right away. This is general guidance, not a substitute for your clinician.

related.title: When to Call the Doctor — Red Flags
related.hook: Most childhood illnesses are mild, but a handful of signs mean don't wait and watch — get medical help right away. Knowing them takes the guesswork out of a scary moment.

related.title: Teething: Signs and Safe Soothing
related.hook: Teething often starts around 6 months, but the timing varies a lot. Expect drooling, gum-rubbing, and fussiness — not a high fever, which points to something else.

choices.text: Skin irritation from contact with urine, stool, and a wet diaper
A bacterial infection that always needs antibiotics

flashcards.explanation_html: Most diaper rash is irritant contact dermatitis — the skin reacting to wetness and rubbing. Keeping the area clean, dry, and aired out usually helps it heal.

flashcards.prompt: What's the 'glass test,' and why does it matter?
flashcards.back_html: Press a clear glass against the rash. If it fades, it's likely harmless. If it does NOT fade (looks like bruises/bleeding under the skin), it's an emergency — call 911/999.

flashcards.prompt: Which rash is the urgent exception that needs immediate care?

choices.text: A rash that doesn't blanch (fade) when you press on it
Diaper rash that improves with diaper changes
A few tiny heat-rash bumps on a warm day

flashcards.explanation_html: A non-blanching rash can signal a serious infection like meningitis or sepsis. It needs immediate medical attention, even if the child otherwise seems okay.
